topic: JVM internals: class loading, memory areas & JIT

questions.question: Your app's class loader is asked to load `java.lang.String`. What happens under the standard parent-delegation model?
options: It searches the app classpath first and asks its parent only if nothing is found there
It delegates to its parent first, so the bootstrap loader ends up defining it
It defines its own private copy, so every loader in the process gets a separate String class
It throws a SecurityException, because app loaders may not resolve any java.* class names
questions.explanation: Parent-first delegation means a loader asks its parent before looking itself, so core classes always come from the bootstrap loader. That keeps a single `String` type for the whole runtime and stops apps from shadowing core classes. Child-first lookup exists in some containers, but it is not the default model.

questions.question: Two different class loaders each load the exact same bytes for `com.app.Plugin`. An object made by loader A is cast to `Plugin` inside code loaded by loader B. What happens?
options: The cast succeeds, because the bytecode and the fully qualified name are identical in both
The cast succeeds, but only if both loaders were created with the same parent loader
ClassCastException: a runtime class is identified by its name plus its defining loader
NoClassDefFoundError: the JVM rejects a second definition of an already loaded class name
questions.explanation: At runtime a class is identified by its binary name together with the loader that defined it, so these are two distinct `Plugin` types. The cast fails with ClassCastException, a classic plugin and hot-reload bug. A shared parent only helps when the class is loaded by that parent, not separately by each child.

questions.question: Class B reads `A.MAX`, where `A.MAX` is declared `static final int MAX = 10;`. This read triggers A's static initializer if A has not been initialized yet.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. A `static final` primitive or String initialized with a compile-time constant is inlined into B's bytecode by the compiler, so B never touches A at runtime and A is not initialized. A side effect is that changing the constant in A without recompiling B leaves B with the old value.

questions.question: What does this Java program print?
options: P then 1
P, C then 1
C, P then 1
1 only
questions.explanation: A static field reference initializes only the class that declares the field. `value` is declared in `Parent`, so `Parent` is initialized (printing P) and `Child` is never initialized even though the source says `Child.value`. If `Child` itself had been initialized, its superclass would have gone first, giving P then C.

questions.question: Inside a method, `int count = 0;` and `User u = new User();` are declared. Where do `count` and the User object live?
options: Both live on the heap; the stack frame only stores return addresses and operands
Both live in the thread's stack frame and are freed together when the method returns
`count` is kept in metaspace with the class, and the User object goes on the heap
`count` and the reference `u` sit in the stack frame; the User object is on the heap
questions.explanation: Local variables, including primitives and object references, are slots in the current thread's stack frame. Objects created with `new` are allocated on the shared heap and outlive the frame if something still references them. Metaspace holds class metadata, not per-call values.

questions.question: A long-running JVM service hits `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` after many plugin reloads, while heap usage looks normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Old class loaders stay reachable, so the classes they defined are never unloaded
Each plugin reload allocates very large arrays that are never released afterwards
String literals from every plugin are interned into metaspace and kept there forever
The JIT code cache overflows and spills compiled methods into metaspace when full
questions.explanation: Metaspace stores class metadata, and classes are unloaded only when their defining loader becomes unreachable. A single lingering reference (a static cache, a thread, a ThreadLocal) to an old loader pins every class it loaded, so each reload leaks a full set. Large arrays would show up as heap pressure, and interned strings live on the heap in modern JVMs.

questions.question: The JIT proves that an object allocated in a hot method never escapes that method or its thread. Which optimizations does this enable? Select all that apply.
options: Promoting the object directly to the old generation to avoid copying
Moving the object's class metadata into the code cache for faster dispatch
Scalar replacement: keeping the object's fields in registers instead of allocating it
Eliding locks taken on that object, since no other thread can see it
questions.explanation: If an object cannot escape, the JIT can break it into its fields (scalar replacement), so no heap allocation happens at all, and it can drop synchronization on it because no other thread can contend. Escape analysis says nothing about class metadata placement, and early promotion is a GC policy, not something non-escaping objects need.

questions.question: Why does HotSpot use tiered compilation (interpreter, then C1, then C2) instead of compiling every method with the optimizing C2 compiler right away?
options: C2 can only compile a method after its class has passed bytecode verification twice
C2's speculative optimizations need profile data, which C1 gathers while giving fast warm-up
C1 emits smaller code, which is required to fit compiled methods into the code cache at all
C2 refuses methods containing loops until the interpreter has run each of them at least once
questions.explanation: C2 is slow to run and bases its aggressive choices (inlining, devirtualization, branch pruning) on observed types and branch frequencies. C1 produces decent code quickly with profiling hooks, so hot code gets fast early and C2 later recompiles it with good data. If a speculation later proves wrong, the method is deoptimized back to a lower tier.

questions.question: Which of these establish a happens-before edge between thread A's action and thread B's later action under the Java memory model? Select all that apply.
options: A writes a volatile field and B later reads that same volatile field
A calls `t.start()` on thread B, and B then runs its first action
A writes a plain field and then calls `Thread.sleep(100)` before B reads it
A releases a monitor and B later acquires the same monitor
A and B both read the same plain field inside a `try/finally` block
questions.explanation: Volatile write to read of the same field, unlock to subsequent lock of the same monitor, and `Thread.start()` to the started thread's actions are all happens-before edges in the JMM. Sleeping gives no ordering guarantee at all, it just makes a race less likely to show. A `try/finally` block has no memory-visibility meaning.

questions.question: Without `volatile` or any synchronization, a thread spinning on `while (!stopped) {}` may never observe another thread setting the plain field `stopped = true`.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. With no happens-before edge, the JIT may hoist the read out of the loop and spin forever on a cached value. Marking the field `volatile` (or using an AtomicBoolean) forces each iteration to observe the latest write.
